Avoid These Common Post-Launch Mistakes Conclusion: Turn Launch Feedback Into Your Next Decision Startups Entrepreneurship Product Management SaaS Aizolo What to Do After Product Launch: A Practical Guide for Founders A practical seven-day plan to understand your first users, fix product problems, and build a repeatable path to growth. Weekly Launches 9 min read · Oct 23, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size weekly launches You have finally finished — your product ready to go out into the world. Your website is up and running, the launch page is set, and your product is announced and shared with your target audience. What now? This is the question that haunts hundreds of project founders at their product launch — and that often leads to disastrous consequences for their business. Finding what to do next is much more challenging than preparing for the launch. During this time, you may get lots of traffic but no users, lots of users but no loyal customers, tons of feedback but no clue what to build next. The truth is, you shouldn’t focus on what to build next or how to promote the product at the very start. First, you need to truly understand your audience, get to the bottom of what they do (or do not) like about your product, and what keeps them from using your product more actively and frequently. Launching your product is only a small step towards product-market fit. Let’s look at how to make this step as useful as possible and what you should prioritize in the crucial first week. 1. Review What Happened During the Launch Press enter or click to view image in full size weekly launches Before planning your next marketing campaign, look at the results of your launch. Start with a few useful metrics: Website visits: How many people reached your website? Traffic sources: Did visitors come from social media, communities, search, or direct links? Sign-ups: How many visitors created an account? Activation: How many new users completed the product’s main action? Conversions: Did anyone start a trial, request a demo, or make a purchase? Each of these figures addresses a different query. One thousand website visits is a nice statistic, but it doesn’t respond to the question of whether the traffic was interested in your product and whether it prompted any engagement. For instance, if your company announced an AI-powered writing tool and scored five hundred hits on the landing page and only five new users, you would want to think about the conversion rate and reconsider the current strategy instead of pumping more money into the marketing campaign. It is possible that the CTR was low because the audience was not interested in your offer or could not grasp what benefits your product brings to the table. Therefore, pick one engaging action that will demonstrate the demand for your product. It could be generating a first report, publishing a website, completing a workflow, or making a first purchase. That action gives you a more useful starting point than page views alone. 2. Talk to Your First Users Press enter or click to view image in full size weekly launches Analytics show what people did, but conversations can help explain why they did it. Reach out personally to users who signed up, tried the product, or abandoned the process. You don’t need an expensive research program. A few thoughtful conversations can reveal problems worth investigating. Ask questions such as: What problem were you trying to solve? What made you try this product? What did you expect it to do? Where did you get stuck? What would make you use it again? Avoid leading questions such as, “Would you use a feature that automatically does this?” People may agree without ever needing the feature. Instead ask them about the workflow it fits in to and what they’ve tried so far. For example if you’re building a project management tool ask them how they do it currently and what frustrates them about their existing process their answer may surprise you revealing that your assumptions were wrong or at least incomplete. Keep in mind that feedback from these early conversations is fuel for research and not necessarily an indication of what your market needs. Seek patterns across multiple customers and compare what they tell you with what you see them doing. And don’t be surprised when what they tell you isn’t what they actually want or need. 3. Fix Friction Before Adding More Features Press enter or click to view image in full size weekly launches After launch, it’s tempting to treat every feature request as a development priority. Resist that temptation until you understand the problem. Users may struggle because: The main benefit isn’t clear. Onboarding requires too many steps. Important instructions are missing. A core workflow is confusing. The product is slow or unreliable. Signup, payment, or integration steps fail. Suppose you launch an AI research tool and immediately start planning team collaboration, advanced exports, and additional integrations. However, new users cannot figure out how to generate their first research report. In that situation, more features won’t solve the immediate problem. A more transparent launch screen, a working prototype, or an improved onboarding experience may be critical to help the users achieve the primary goal. Focus on resolving the most common obstacles to achieving the primary objectives. Make sure the software serves its purpose right away and then look into the secondary and tertiary ones.
